Passage A

[1] Mrs. Okafor had forbidden the Elgar. "You have played it four hundred times," she said on Thursday, packing her own instrument into its case as though the lesson were already over. "Tomorrow you will play it the four hundred and first. Tonight you will not touch it." Then she wrote on the back of an envelope what I was permitted: scales in C and D, slow, with the metronome at sixty, and nothing else.

[2] I lasted until nine o'clock. My cello stood in the corner of the dining room where it always stood, its case open, and from the table where I was pretending to read I could see the scroll catching the lamp. The audition was at ten the next morning, in a room I had seen only in a photograph on the conservatory's website: pale wood, one chair, three people behind a long table.

[3] I told myself that scales were not cheating. I set the metronome ticking and played C major up four octaves and down, and it sounded like what it was, a girl playing scales in a dining room. D major was the same. Somewhere in the second octave of D, my left hand began to drift toward the opening of the first movement, the way your feet drift toward a house you used to live in. I stopped with the bow on the string.

[4] What I did instead surprised me. I took the envelope off the music stand, turned it over, and on the front, under the electric company's window, I wrote out the first four bars of the Elgar from memory. Not the notes, which I could not have lost if I tried, but the fingerings, the bowings, the one place where I breathe. It took twenty minutes. When I finished, I found I had written a breath mark in the third bar, where I had never once taken a breath.

[5] I looked at it for a long time. Then I put the cello in its case, closed the latches one at a time, and went to bed with the envelope under my pillow like a child with a tooth.

Passage B

[6] The track at Linwood stayed open until dusk, and Dev went down after supper without telling his sister, who had coached him since he was eleven and who believed, as an article of faith, that the night before a final belongs to the couch. He did not mean to run. He wore jeans so that he couldn't.

[7] The 1500 meters was three and three-quarter laps, and he walked them. He started where the race would start, on the curve, and walked the first two hundred in the outside half of lane one, where Priya always told him to stay out of trouble. At the bell he stopped and stood there, on the spot where in eighteen hours a bell would ring and the whole field would wind up and someone would try to go past him on the back straight.

[8] He had raced this distance thirty-one times. He knew, from Priya's spreadsheet, that he had won twelve of the races in which he led at the bell and two of the races in which he did not. He had always taken the number as an instruction: be in front at the bell. Standing on the spot, he understood it differently. The races he had led at the bell were the races in which he had already felt good. The lead was not a cause; it was a symptom.

[9] He did not know what to do with that. It seemed like the kind of thing a person should not find out the night before. He finished the lap at a walk anyway, and on the last straight, where his legs would be burning, he counted his steps from the final turn to the line—eighty-four, in jeans—and decided that the number was his, and that he would not tell Priya about it.

[10] When he got home she was on the couch with the spreadsheet open on her laptop. "Where were you?" she asked. "Walking," he said, which was true.

choices: The first four bars of the Elgar, played very slowly
Scales in any key the narrator wished to choose
Nothing at all, since she was to rest the cello
Slow scales in two keys, played with the metronome
correct_answer: Slow scales in two keys, played with the metronome
explanation: Mrs. Okafor writes on the envelope what is permitted: "scales in C and D, slow, with the metronome at sixty, and nothing else" - slow scales in two keys with the metronome. The Elgar is exactly what she "had forbidden" ("Tonight you will not touch it"), so playing its opening is ruled out. The keys are named, C and D, so the narrator could not choose any key. And she was permitted something, the scales, so complete rest is not what was allowed.

passage_title: The Bump in the Middle of Memory
passage:
[1] Ask a seventy-year-old to tell you about her life, and you will not get an even record. Ask her instead to respond to a list of ordinary words—"river," "letter," "kitchen"—with the first personal memory each word brings to mind, then to date each memory, and a shape emerges that psychologists have found in study after study. Memories from the last few years are plentiful, as you would expect; forgetting has had little time to work on them. Memories from early childhood are scarce. But between the two, instead of a smooth decline, the curve rises again into a hump: people over about forty recall a disproportionate number of events from roughly the ages of ten to thirty. Researchers call it the reminiscence bump.

[2] The word-cue method behind these curves is old—a version of it was used by the Victorian scientist Francis Galton—but the bump itself was named only in the 1980s, when researchers pooling several sets of data noticed that the excess of youthful memories did not go away when the cue words or the people being tested were changed. It appears when people are asked for their most important memories, and it appears for more trivial things too: the books, films, and songs people name as their favorites tend to come from the same stretch of years.

[3] Why should a few years in the middle of a life take up so much room? The first explanation offered was about novelty. Adolescence and early adulthood are crowded with firsts—first job, first apartment, first time living away from home—and an event that has no precedent is distinctive, rehearsed, and hard to confuse with others. Routine, by contrast, wears a groove in which one day can hardly be told from the next. Later Tuesdays blur together; the first Tuesday at a new job does not.

[4] A second explanation shifts the emphasis from the events to the person remembering them. On this account, those years are when a stable identity is assembled, and memories that help define who someone is get kept, retold, and linked to one another. The memories survive not because the events were new but because they became part of the story the person tells about himself or herself.

[5] Both accounts were challenged by a simple observation: the bump is lopsided. When people are asked for happy memories, the bump appears clearly. When they are asked for sad or frightening ones, it largely disappears; those memories are spread more evenly across the lifespan. Novelty cannot easily explain this, since a first grief is as novel as a first love. Nor is it obvious why an identity would be assembled only from pleasant material.

[6] The explanation that fits the lopsidedness best is cultural. Within a given culture, people share a rough script for how a life is supposed to go—when one leaves school, falls in love, starts work, marries, has children. When researchers ask people, even fairly young ones, to imagine a typical life and to name its important events, the events cluster in the same years as the bump, and nearly all of them are expected to be happy. The script, on this view, works like a set of folders: it tells memory where to look. Events that the script anticipates are easier to find when someone searches. Unscripted events, which include most misfortunes, have no folder, and they are retrieved without that advantage wherever in life they fell.

[7] None of the three accounts has been retired. The cultural script says nothing about why favorite songs come from the same years, which seems closer to the novelty account, and it is plausible that the script itself exists partly because those years really are full of first times. What the debate has done is change the question. Asking when an event happened has turned out to be less useful than asking how a person goes about finding it, because a memory that cannot be found is, for the purposes of a life story, the same as one that was never stored.

passage:
[1] For most of the history of printing, a typeface was not an idea but a heap of metal. A printer who owned a face owned thousands of small blocks of lead alloy, called sorts, each carrying one raised letter in reverse, along with the punches and matrices from which more could be cast. To speak of a printer's type was to speak of something that could be weighed, counted, borrowed, and stolen. It is worth holding on to that fact, because it is what makes the strangest episode in the history of English book design legible at all.

[2] The Doves Press opened in Hammersmith, on the Thames west of central London, in 1900. Its two partners were T. J. Cobden-Sanderson, a former barrister who had become a bookbinder, and Emery Walker, an engraver and printer with a deep knowledge of early type. Their press had one typeface, cut in one size, modelled on a roman used by the Venetian printer Nicolas Jenson in the 1470s. It had no italic and no bold. The books were set without illustration, with wide margins and occasional calligraphic initials in red, and their most admired production, a five-volume Bible, was praised precisely for what it left out.

[3] The partnership did not last. The two men disagreed about money and about control, and the arrangement they reached for winding up the press left the fate of the type unsettled in a way that, from Walker's side, meant he expected eventually to use it. Cobden-Sanderson had other ideas. Beginning in 1916, when he was in his late seventies, he walked out onto Hammersmith Bridge at night, many nights over several months, and dropped the press's equipment into the river: first the punches and matrices, then the sorts themselves, a little at a time. He recorded the work in his journal in the language of ceremony, writing of the type as a bequest to the river.

[4] It is easy to call this vandalism, and Walker, who eventually took the matter to law, plainly did. But it is more interesting to ask what Cobden-Sanderson thought he was preventing. He was not destroying books; every Doves volume already printed was untouched, and he seems to have regarded those books as the type's real and finished work. What he feared was the face going on without him—set by other hands, in books he had not chosen, pressed into service it had not been made for. On his view, a typeface was inseparable from the press that used it, the way a voice is inseparable from a speaker. Sink the metal and the voice would stop.

[5] The century that followed proved him wrong in a way he could not have imagined. Once type became a matter of drawings, then of film, and finally of digital outlines, a face stopped being a heap of anything. It became information, and information does not sink. In the early 2010s a designer named Robert Green spent years redrawing the Doves type from printed pages, and then, with the help of divers working for the Port of London Authority, searched the riverbed below the bridge. They brought up a modest number of the original sorts—around a hundred and fifty, out of the many thousands thrown in. Green used them to correct his drawings. The face that Cobden-Sanderson meant to end is now a file that anyone may buy.

[6] There is an irony here, but it is not a simple one. Cobden-Sanderson was right that the metal and the meaning had been bound together; he was wrong only about which of them would outlast the other. The recovered sorts are treasured now for exactly the reason he would have given: they were the press's own. The file, by contrast, carries the letterforms without the margins, the red initials, the long silences of the Bible. It is the voice without the speaker. Whether that is the type surviving or only the type's ghost depends on which of two beliefs you hold: that a face is its shapes, or that a face is what it was used for.

[1] In the 1960s, a field biologist working in Amboseli, in southern Kenya, noticed that vervet monkeys did not have a single alarm call. They had several, and the one a monkey gave seemed to depend on what it had seen. A leopard drew a loud, barking call; a martial eagle, a short, low, coughing one; a python, a high chatter. Each call was followed by a different response. Monkeys that heard the leopard call ran up into the trees, where a leopard, which hunts on the ground and ambushes from cover, has a harder time. At the eagle call they looked up and dashed into dense bushes, out of reach of a bird that strikes from above. At the snake call they stood on their hind legs and peered at the grass around them.

[2] The observation was striking, but it did not show what it seemed to show. A monkey that sees a leopard and runs up a tree may be responding to the leopard, not to the call. Its companions may have seen the leopard too, or may simply be copying the caller's flight. For the calls to count as signals that carried information about the predator, someone had to separate the sound from everything else that happens when a predator appears. Watching alone, however patiently, could not tell these possibilities apart.

[3] That was done in the late 1970s by a team who recorded alarm calls and played them back from loudspeakers hidden in the bushes when no predator was present. The design was simple and the results were clean. Played the leopard call, the monkeys ran for the trees. Played the eagle call, they looked up, and many ran into cover. Played the snake call, they rose and looked down. The responses followed the recording, not the scene, and so the information had to be in the sound.

[4] The researchers also checked a less interesting possibility. Leopard alarms tend to be louder and longer than eagle alarms, so perhaps the monkeys were not distinguishing kinds of call at all, only degrees of urgency—a loud call meaning "climb," a soft one meaning "hide." When the team compared playbacks of different types that were matched in length and loudness, the responses still followed the type. What mattered was which call it was, not how alarming it sounded.

[5] It would be easy to describe these calls as words, and popular accounts often do. Researchers who study them are more careful. They describe such alarms as functionally referential: calls that are reliably linked to a class of things in the world and that cause listeners to behave as though that thing were present. The phrase is deliberately limited. It describes what the calls do, and it leaves open what, if anything, the caller intends, or whether a monkey giving the leopard alarm has anything in mind resembling the idea "leopard."

[6] Young vervets help show where the calls come from. Infants give alarm calls, but they give them too broadly: an infant may give the eagle alarm at almost anything that flies, including harmless birds and, by one report, a falling leaf. With age the range narrows until it matches that of adults, centered on the few species that actually hunt monkeys. The basic sounds seem to be inborn; experience sharpens what they are used for. Adults appear to help in an indirect way, more often answering an infant's alarm with alarms of their own when the infant has called at a genuinely dangerous bird.

[7] The vervet work changed the questions asked about other animals. Researchers have since reported predator-specific calls in some birds, in meerkats, and in other primates, though the strength of the evidence varies from species to species and some of the claims are disputed. What has lasted is less a particular finding than a method: before deciding what a call means, take away the caller and the predator and see whether the sound alone is enough.
